lede: Several forces pulling one body can always be replaced by a single force that would do exactly the same job. That single force is the resultant, and finding it is the same two-column arithmetic every time: total across, total up.
can: Find the resultant of two or more forces given in i and j form
Resolve forces given at angles and total the two directions
Work out the magnitude and the direction of a resultant

md: Three people push a stalled car from slightly different angles. The car does not feel three pushes: it feels one, in one direction, of one size. That single equivalent force is what the resultant means.

md:
The resultant is the single force that has the same effect as the whole set. It has a size and a direction, so an answer is never finished until both are given, or until it is written in $\mathbf{i}$ and $\mathbf{j}$ form.

Forces pulling in different directions never simply add up: $30 + 24 + 10$ is not the answer to anything here.

prompt: Three forces of 30 N, 24 N and 10 N act at a point in different directions. What can be said about the size of their resultant?
explain: Only forces pointing exactly the same way add to their total. Pulling in different directions, some of each force works against the others.

text: 2. In i and j, total the two columns

alt: A table of three forces written in i and j with their across and up parts listed: 9 and minus 4, minus 5 and 7, and 8 and 2. The bottom row totals the two columns to give a resultant of 12 across and 5 up.

md:
When the forces are given in components the work is arithmetic: total the $\mathbf{i}$ parts, total the $\mathbf{j}$ parts, and keep the two columns apart.

Watch the negatives. Adding $-5$ takes five away, and subtracting a force instead of adding it is a slip the reports have seen in this question.

prompt: Two forces are $(8\mathbf{i} - 3\mathbf{j})$ N and $(-5\mathbf{i} + 7\mathbf{j})$ N. What is their resultant?
explain: $8 - 5 = 3$ across and $-3 + 7 = 4$ up, so the resultant is $3\mathbf{i} + 4\mathbf{j}$ N.

text: 3. Forces at angles: resolve, then total

md:
Forces given at angles have to be resolved before they can be combined. Choose two perpendicular directions, take to the right and upwards as positive, and resolve every force into those.

Here the across total is $30 + 24\cos 50° - 10 = 35.43$ N and the up total is $24\sin 50° = 18.39$ N.

prompt: A force of 20 N acts horizontally to the right and a force of 6 N acts horizontally to the left. What is the total component to the right, in newtons?
explain: The second force points the other way, so it is subtracted: $20 - 6 = 14$ N.

alt: A right-angled triangle. The horizontal side is labelled 16 N across, the vertical side 12 N up, and the sloping side, drawn as a solid arrow from the corner, is labelled R. The angle between R and the horizontal side is marked.

caption: The two totals are the legs; the resultant is the longest side.

md:
The across total and the up total are at right angles, so they are the two shorter sides of a right-angled triangle and the resultant is its longest side.

That makes the magnitude $\sqrt{X^2 + Y^2}$, which is on the Unit 2 formula sheet as the magnitude of $x\mathbf{i} + y\mathbf{j}$. With totals of $16$ N and $12$ N it is $\sqrt{256 + 144} = 20$ N.

title: A-Level Maths: R1-12 Forces: Finding the Magnitude and Direction of a Resultant Force
why: The two totals, then Pythagoras, then the angle, worked at a slower pace. Watch the diagram being drawn before either calculation starts.

prompt: The forces on a body have a total component of 8 N to the right and 6 N upwards. What is the magnitude of the resultant, in newtons?
explain: $\sqrt{8^2 + 6^2} = \sqrt{100} = 10$ N. The two totals are perpendicular, so Pythagoras applies.

text: 5. The direction, and the line it is measured from

caption: The angle is measured from the line the question names.

md:
In the same triangle the up total is opposite the angle and the across total is beside it, so $\tan\theta = \dfrac{Y}{X}$ and $\theta = \tan^{-1}\dfrac{Y}{X}$.

That is the angle with the horizontal, which is the line these questions almost always name. Turn the fraction over and you get the angle with the vertical instead, which is a different answer to a different question.

title: Why the fraction goes that way up
md: Tangent is opposite over adjacent. Measuring from the horizontal makes the up total the opposite side and the across total the adjacent one, so the up total goes on top. Sketching the triangle and marking the angle settles it every time.

prompt: A resultant has a total component of $X$ to the right and $Y$ upwards. Which expression gives the angle it makes with the horizontal?
explain: The up total is opposite the angle and the across total is beside it, so the up total is on top. The second option is the angle with the vertical.

md:
Add forces given in i and j by totalling the two columns, negatives included.
Resolve forces given at angles and total the across and up directions separately.
Find the magnitude of a resultant from its two totals with Pythagoras.
Find its direction with an inverse tangent, and say which line the angle is measured from.

Question 1 or 2 gives forces in i and j, or at angles, and asks for the resultant, then its magnitude for 2 to 4 marks and its direction for 2. The first mark is for the two totals written down; the last is for the angle to 2 decimal places, measured from the line the question names. Stuck? Write the across total and the up total on separate lines before anything else.
